# Maths S11 D03: Which sampling method gives a sample that represents the population? Census and sample; random, systematic, stratified and self-selected samples compared; and judging a sample by how it was chosen (design)

Status: Revision 3 (25 Nov 2026): preflight and fact repairs (see the final section, "Revision 3 (root, 25 November 2026)"). Revision 2 (24 Nov 2026): learning review resolved (see "Revision 2" below); not voiced. Revision 1 (24 Nov 2026): first design, written to the maths visual standard (`../maths-visual-standard.md`), `math-s11-d01.md` and `d02.md` (Revision 1, this batch), the Year 12 design that recalls this video (`math-s12-p08.md`: "Year 11 d03 (samples; random and self-selected samples)"), the coherence audit and root's Standard rulings 1 to 99. Not voiced. Next: student learning review and Codex maths check, then voicing on the Google voice and a build on the studio kit to grade A.

Narration 5,516 characters by script (see "Narration length estimate"; Revision 2), 13 scene headings, about 496 s with holds (key notes fixed at 45 s). Nothing recorded; human listening pending.

Scope: third video of the Year 11 Data analysis strand, outline playlist order 63. One video for Standard 1 and Standard 2. Viewers arrive from d02's final frame. Pre-design pack: `../pre-design/maths-standard/math-s11-d03.md`. Route entry: `math-s11-d03` in `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`. Site lessons: `year11/data-analysis/lesson02.sa.html` (card 05, WE, drill 5) and `lesson09.sa.html` (card 06, MC 2, MC 4, trap 02). Visual system: maths studio kit; the bus, calculator, tournament board, paper sheet and concert ticket plates (all existing); the dot field sampler, list pointer and comparison table coded.

Owner rules applied: as d01 (header strip "DATA ANALYSIS" only; one question; one stage at a time; plain meanings; two attempts with "Pause here to answer." and 10 s countdowns; brief feedback with one crossed slip; five key notes with a framed card; everyday anchors; no people, hands or faces (dots and tokens only); Australian spelling; no em dashes).

Syllabus content points (Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11, Data analysis, "Population and sample", common to Standard 1 and Standard 2), quoted from `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`:

- `ci3d27ce1c`: "Compare and contrast systematic sampling, self-selected sampling, random sampling and stratified sampling"
- `ciefb0c944`: "Justify whether a sample obtained from a population is representative of the population by considering the sampling method"

Source: https://curriculum.nsw.edu.au/learning-areas/mathematics/mathematics-standard-11-12-2024/content/year-11/fa4de413b8

**Boundary:** starts from d02's final frame exactly (the 200-dot field, about 1,000 px wide, 140 dots blue and 60 dots blue with amber outlines; legend chips "140 live nearby" and "60 catch the early bus"; counter "sample: 20"; the bus `ma12-bus-side-v1.png`, about 420 px wide, at the bottom right; chips "Who do we ask?", "Next: sampling methods" and "?"). Recalls d01 (target population, sample) and d02 (bias as a lean) in grey chips. Teaches: census and sample; representative; random, systematic, stratified and self-selected sampling (convenience named once); comparing them; justifying representativeness by the method. Not taught: faults in experiments and observational studies (d04).

## Revision 2: learning review resolved (24 Nov 2026)

Source review: `../checks/m-s11-d03-learning-review.md`; resolution record `../checks/m-s11-d-learning-review-resolution.md`.

- **D03-RAN (note): applied.** The calculator screen in scene 2 reads "random: 137", not the brand key label "Ran#". No narration changed.
- Narration 5,528 characters (Revision 1: 5,528); about 497 s with holds, under the 570 s cap. Both attempts still end "Pause here to answer."; feedback about 26.5 s and 23.0 s. No em dash. Joins unchanged.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the early bus (d02's frame).** Bus students get up earlier, so they may sleep less. A sample with too few or too many of them would lean the results. That gives "representative" a concrete meaning: the sample should look like the population in the ways that matter for the question (here, where students live).
- **One sampler, four methods (recurring model).** The 200-dot field is the population for every method, so the methods differ only in how dots are chosen. Order: census (1 sentence), random, systematic, stratified, self-selected; then a comparison.
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Census ("collecting data from every member of the population"); representative ("a sample that looks like the population in the ways that matter for the question"); random sample ("every member has the same chance of being chosen"); systematic sample ("choose every k-th member from a list, after a random start"); stratified sample ("split the population into groups, then randomly choose from each group in proportion to its size"); self-selected sample ("people choose to take part themselves"); convenience ("asking whoever is easiest to reach", one sentence).
- **Random runs vary (visual surprise).** Three runs of the random sampler give 4, 9 and 6 bus students (example seeds; 6 is the fair share). Random is fair, but a small random sample can be unlucky. Stratified gives 14 and 6 every time.
- **Systematic step.** k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10 with a random start from 1 to 10 (start 7 shown: 7, 17, 27, ..., 197). One sentence on a patterned list (if the roll listed every tenth student as a bus student, the step could pick only them or none).
- **Self-selected (example data).** A poster with a QR code on the tournament board: 20 replies, 14 slept under 7 hours. Tired students had more reason to answer. A bigger self-selected sample would still lean.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Dot field sampler** (scenes 2 to 5): the population field with modes: random (20 dots light one at a time, a stratum counter "bus: n of 20"; a "run again" pulse); systematic (a numbered list strip beside the field, a pointer stepping by 10 from a random start); stratified (the field splits into two labelled blocks, each drawing its share); self-selected (dots answer only if they "choose", weighted towards amber-tired dots; reply counter).
  2. **Share bar** (scenes 2 to 6): under the field, a bar showing the sample's bus share against the population's 30% line.
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red. Here: population dots blue; bus students blue with amber outlines (the same as d02's frame); chosen dots glow green-outlined; the 30% fair-share line amber.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "everyone = census", "same chance", "unlucky, not unfair", "every 10th", "groups in proportion", "14 + 6 every time", "who chose to answer?", "bigger, still leaning", "judge the method". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The population and bus (1); census and random (2); systematic with the list (3); stratified blocks (4); self-selected poster (5); comparison table (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the headline and split tokens (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 3: "k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10"; "start 7: 7, 17, 27, ..., 197" (framed green). Scene 4: task strip "Stratified sample of 20 from 140 nearby and 60 bus students."; rows "nearby: 140 ÷ 200 × 20 = 14", "bus: 60 ÷ 200 × 20 = 6" (framed green); crossed slip "10 nearby and 10 bus" (caption "in proportion, not equal").
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Random gives everyone the same chance. Stratified keeps the groups in proportion." Key line: "Judge a sample by how it was chosen, not by how big it is."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): 24 and 16; reason; crossed "20 juniors and 20 seniors" (caption "in proportion: 180 of 300"). A2 (pack question 2): systematic, self-selected, random; the poll least representative; crossed "(i) random" (caption "a fixed step: systematic").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Equal strata (4, A1); self-selected mistaken for random (5, A2); "bigger fixes it" (5); everyday "random" (2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a census is complete but slow and costly, so we usually sample, and the sample only helps if it looks like the population (2); (2) giving every member the same chance removes the investigator's lean, but chance alone can still give a lopsided small sample (2); (3) a fixed step through a list spreads the sample out, as long as the list's order isn't linked to the answer (3); (4) choosing from each group in proportion guarantees the groups that matter are represented fairly (4); (5) volunteers choose themselves for a reason, often a strong feeling, so their answers lean, however many there are (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (target population, sample), d02 (bias; the 140 and 60), Stage 4 percentages. Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** lesson02 and lesson09 values recalculated: no arithmetic error. MSY-35 (lesson02's call-in item).
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d04, faults in data collection).** Scene 12: board clear; the bedroom `ms12-bedroom-furniture-v1.png` (about 900 px wide) at the left with a coded headline card above it (white card, 44 px): "Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!"; at the right the 20 sample tokens in two olive-labelled groups "phone in bedroom: 12" and "elsewhere: 8"; chips "What could go wrong?", "Next: faults in data collection" and "?". d04 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) 140 ÷ 200 = 0.7; 0.7 × 20 = 14; 60 ÷ 200 = 0.3; 0.3 × 20 = 6.
  (b) 200 ÷ 20 = 10; start 7: 7 + 10 × 19 = 197 (20 positions).
  (c) Random runs (builder fixes seeds): 4, 9, 6 bus students of 20.
  (d) Self-selected example: 20 replies, 14 under 7 h (labelled "example").
  (e) A1: 180 ÷ 300 = 0.6, × 40 = 24; 120 ÷ 300 = 0.4, × 40 = 16; 24 + 16 = 40.

Main question: *Sixty of the two hundred catch the early bus. Which twenty do we ask, so the sample looks like the population?*
Entry knowledge (math-s11-d01, d02; Stage 4): target population, sample; bias; percentages of an amount.
Stops after: census; four methods compared; representativeness justified by the method.
Handoff: math-s11-d04: "Next: faults in data collection".

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour roles (fixed): values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread amber; answer green; mistake red. Header strip "DATA ANALYSIS", with the mini investigation strip ("collect" lit). Scene headings in the hand font, 44 px.

teaching.task: # Maths S11 D03: Which sampling method gives a sample that represents the population? Census and sample; random, systematic, stratified and self-selected samples compared; and judging a sample by how it was chosen (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Asking every member of the population is called a census. It's the most complete, but it takes time and money, and for big populations it's often impossible. So we sample. And a sample is only useful if it's representative, meaning it looks like the population in the ways that matter for our question. Here, that's where students live. The first method is a random sample, where every member has the same chance of being chosen. That's not the everyday meaning of random, just grabbing whoever. It means a fair draw, like a random number generator on a calculator, picking students by their roll numbers. Let's run it. This draw picked four bus students. Run it again, nine. Again, six. Random sampling is fair, because nobody chooses who's in. But with a small sample, chance can still give you a lopsided one. A systematic sample picks every k-th member from a list. Divide the population by the sample size. Two hundred divided by twenty is ten, so we take every tenth student on the roll. Start at a random place between one and ten, say seven. Then seven, seventeen, twenty-seven, and so on, up to one ninety-seven. That's twenty students, spread evenly through the list. It's quick, and it usually behaves like a random sample. The catch is a list with a pattern. If every tenth student on the roll happened to be a bus student, a step of ten could pick all bus students, or none. A stratified sample makes sure the groups that matter are there in the right amounts. Split the population into groups, then randomly choose from each group in proportion to its size. A hundred and forty of two hundred is seventy per cent, so seventy per cent of twenty, fourteen students from nearby. Sixty of two hundred is thirty per cent, so six bus students. Then choose the fourteen and the six at random. Every run gives fourteen and six, so the bus students are always fairly represented. A common slip is ten from each group. That gives bus students far more say than their share of the year.

teaching.openingDecision: Visual: opens on d02's final frame exactly. On "we want to ask twenty" the "Next" chips fade and the counter "sample: 20" pulses. On "might sleep less" the bus plate nudges and the 60 amber-outlined dots pulse. teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn. A sports club has three hundred members, a hundred and eighty juniors and a hundred and twenty seniors. How many of each belong in a stratified sample of forty? Then give one reason a stratified sample is more likely to represent the club than an online poll that members choose to answer. Pause here to answer. Last one. Name the sampling method in each case. One, every fiftieth ticket scanned at a concert gate. Two, a poll on the band's website. Three, names drawn by a random number generator from the ticket list. Which is least likely to be representative, and why? Pause here to answer.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the early bus (d02's frame).** Bus students get up earlier, so they may sleep less. A sample with too few or too many of them would lean the results. That gives "representative" a concrete meaning: the sample should look like the population in the ways that matter for the question (here, where students live).
- **One sampler, four methods (recurring model).** The 200-dot field is the population for every method, so the methods differ only in how dots are chosen. Order: census (1 sentence), random, systematic, stratified, self-selected; then a comparison.
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Census ("collecting data from every member of the population"); representative ("a sample that looks like the population in the ways that matter for the question"); random sample ("every member has the same chance of being chosen"); systematic sample ("choose every k-th member from a list, after a random start"); stratified sample ("split the population into groups, then randomly choose from each group in proportion to its size"); self-selected sample ("people choose to take part themselves"); convenience ("asking whoever is easiest to reach", one sentence).
- **Random runs vary (visual surprise).** Three runs of the random sampler give 4, 9 and 6 bus students (example seeds; 6 is the fair share). Random is fair, but a small random sample can be unlucky. Stratified gives 14 and 6 every time.
- **Systematic step.** k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10 with a random start from 1 to 10 (start 7 shown: 7, 17, 27, ..., 197). One sentence on a patterned list (if the roll listed every tenth student as a bus student, the step could pick only them or none).
- **Self-selected (example data).** A poster with a QR code on the tournament board: 20 replies, 14 slept under 7 hours. Tired students had more reason to answer. A bigger self-selected sample would still lean.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Dot field sampler** (scenes 2 to 5): the population field with modes: random (20 dots light one at a time, a stratum counter "bus: n of 20"; a "run again" pulse); systematic (a numbered list strip beside the field, a pointer stepping by 10 from a random start); stratified (the field splits into two labelled blocks, each drawing its share); self-selected (dots answer only if they "choose", weighted towards amber-tired dots; reply counter).
  2. **Share bar** (scenes 2 to 6): under the field, a bar showing the sample's bus share against the population's 30% line.
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red. Here: population dots blue; bus students blue with amber outlines (the same as d02's frame); chosen dots glow green-outlined; the 30% fair-share line amber.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "everyone = census", "same chance", "unlucky, not unfair", "every 10th", "groups in proportion", "14 + 6 every time", "who chose to answer?", "bigger, still leaning", "judge the method". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The population and bus (1); census and random (2); systematic with the list (3); stratified blocks (4); self-selected poster (5); comparison table (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the headline and split tokens (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 3: "k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10"; "start 7: 7, 17, 27, ..., 197" (framed green). Scene 4: task strip "Stratified sample of 20 from 140 nearby and 60 bus students."; rows "nearby: 140 ÷ 200 × 20 = 14", "bus: 60 ÷ 200 × 20 = 6" (framed green); crossed slip "10 nearby and 10 bus" (caption "in proportion, not equal").
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Random gives everyone the same chance. Stratified keeps the groups in proportion." Key line: "Judge a sample by how it was chosen, not by how big it is."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): 24 and 16; reason; crossed "20 juniors and 20 seniors" (caption "in proportion: 180 of 300"). A2 (pack question 2): systematic, self-selected, random; the poll least representative; crossed "(i) random" (caption "a fixed step: systematic").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Equal strata (4, A1); self-selected mistaken for random (5, A2); "bigger fixes it" (5); everyday "random" (2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a census is complete but slow and costly, so we usually sample, and the sample only helps if it looks like the population (2); (2) giving every member the same chance removes the investigator's lean, but chance alone can still give a lopsided small sample (2); (3) a fixed step through a list spreads the sample out, as long as the list's order isn't linked to the answer (3); (4) choosing from each group in proportion guarantees the groups that matter are represented fairly (4); (5) volunteers choose themselves for a reason, often a strong feeling, so their answers lean, however many there are (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (target population, sample), d02 (bias; the 140 and 60), Stage 4 percentages. Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** lesson02 and lesson09 values recalculated: no arithmetic error. MSY-35 (lesson02's call-in item).
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d04, faults in data collection).** Scene 12: board clear; the bedroom `ms12-bedroom-furniture-v1.png` (about 900 px wide) at the left with a coded headline card above it (white card, 44 px): "Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!"; at the right the 20 sample tokens in two olive-labelled groups "phone in bedroom: 12" and "elsewhere: 8"; chips "What could go wrong?", "Next: faults in data collection" and "?". d04 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) 140 ÷ 200 = 0.7; 0.7 × 20 = 14; 60 ÷ 200 = 0.3; 0.3 × 20 = 6.
  (b) 200 ÷ 20 = 10; start 7: 7 + 10 × 19 = 197 (20 positions).
  (c) Random runs (builder fixes seeds): 4, 9, 6 bus students of 20.
  (d) Self-selected example: 20 replies, 14 under 7 h (labelled "example").
  (e) A1: 180 ÷ 300 = 0.6, × 40 = 24; 120 ÷ 300 = 0.4, × 40 = 16; 24 + 16 = 40.

Main question: *Sixty of the two hundred catch the early bus. Which twenty do we ask, so the sample looks like the population?*

scenes.teachingReason: Two hundred Year 11 students, and we want to ask twenty. Sixty of them catch the early bus, so they get up sooner, and they might sleep less. If our twenty were mostly bus students, our results would make the whole year look more tired than it is. If there were none, it would look less tired. Either way, the sample wouldn't look like the population. So which sampling method gives a sample that represents the population?

scenes.teachingReason: Asking every member of the population is called a census. It's the most complete, but it takes time and money, and for big populations it's often impossible. So we sample. And a sample is only useful if it's representative, meaning it looks like the population in the ways that matter for our question. Here, that's where students live. The first method is a random sample, where every member has the same chance of being chosen. That's not the everyday meaning of random, just grabbing whoever. It means a fair draw, like a random number generator on a calculator, picking students by their roll numbers. Let's run it. This draw picked four bus students. Run it again, nine. Again, six. Random sampling is fair, because nobody chooses who's in. But with a small sample, chance can still give you a lopsided one.

scenes.teachingReason: A systematic sample picks every k-th member from a list. Divide the population by the sample size. Two hundred divided by twenty is ten, so we take every tenth student on the roll. Start at a random place between one and ten, say seven. Then seven, seventeen, twenty-seven, and so on, up to one ninety-seven. That's twenty students, spread evenly through the list. It's quick, and it usually behaves like a random sample. The catch is a list with a pattern. If every tenth student on the roll happened to be a bus student, a step of ten could pick all bus students, or none.

scenes.teachingReason: A stratified sample makes sure the groups that matter are there in the right amounts. Split the population into groups, then randomly choose from each group in proportion to its size. A hundred and forty of two hundred is seventy per cent, so seventy per cent of twenty, fourteen students from nearby. Sixty of two hundred is thirty per cent, so six bus students. Then choose the fourteen and the six at random. Every run gives fourteen and six, so the bus students are always fairly represented. A common slip is ten from each group. That gives bus students far more say than their share of the year.

scenes.teachingReason: The last method is a self-selected sample, where people choose to take part themselves. Say we pin a poster in the corridor. Scan this code to tell us about your sleep. Twenty replies come in, and fourteen say they slept under seven hours. Does that mean most of Year 11 is short on sleep? Not necessarily. Students who feel tired have a reason to answer, and students who sleep well might walk straight past. The sample chose itself, so it leans. And getting two hundred replies wouldn't fix it. A bigger self-selected sample still leans the same way. Asking whoever's easiest to reach, like the canteen queue, called a convenience sample, has the same problem.

scenes.teachingReason: So how do they compare? Random gives everyone the same chance, but a small sample can be unlucky. Systematic is quick and spreads out, if the list has no pattern. Stratified guarantees the groups that matter are in proportion, but you need to know the groups first. Self-selected is easy, but it leans towards people with strong feelings. To justify whether a sample is representative, look at how it was chosen. Did every member, or every group, get a fair chance? For our sleep survey, stratified is the best choice, because where students live affects when they wake up.
